2026: 2026 was also the culmination year of a longer story. The Woods Stage moves through roughly seven-year cycles of growth before it’s brought down and reinvented: it’s been reborn about four times since Pickathon’s start at Pendarvis Farm. 2026 marks the current cycle’s zenith, its fullest flower, before the next rebirth begins.
For 2026, Scott Edwards Architecture (SEA) presents Synthesis, a stage concept built around a modular system originally designed for the future expansion of Portland’s Q-Side Skatepark in Old Town.

After Pickathon 2026, the modular parts from the stage were set to be repurposed for their intended destination, Q-Side Skatepark, extending the life of the project beyond the festival and back into Portland’s Old Town neighborhood.

The 2026 theme drew on the power and rhythms of the ocean, and the nets at the heart of the fishing industry. As the primary material for the 2026 stage, disused fishing nets form cylindrical shapes on land, stretched and draped from elevated towers reminiscent of carrelet fishing huts, intermingling with the tall trees behind the stage. Their knotty, undulating surfaces catch and reflect light behind the performers, while strategic uplights reveal the large implied volumes. The ocean currents that once moved these nets underwater become, in this context, musical waves , the nets filtering light, sound, views, and movement, creating moments of opacity and transparency, enclosure and openness. In the same way water moves through a net and reaches the shore, sound moves through the installation and reaches the human body.

The 2026 stage took reuse further: once the nets have served at Cherry Hill, the maritime recycling nonprofit Net Your Problem will ship them to Ukraine, where they’ll be repurposed to protect villages from drone attacks: nets that once caught fish, and provided livelihoods for Oregon fishermen, going on to save lives in a war zone. In between, they’ll form a venue where the Pickathon community gathers for a weekend of music and togetherness. A net is made through connection: each strand depends on the others, forming a larger system of support and collective strength , reflecting the values at the heart of the festival.
Design Team: Professor Travis Bell, Timothy Boscacci, Courtney Frederick, Russ Golubev, Isabelle Jones, Jake Muldoon, Anthony Westwolf

Designed by WORKS Architecture, C.H.A.D. and the locals feel the pull: something out there is drawing them in. Explore the neighborhood and find C.H.A.D. (Curious Happenings Anomaly Detection) among the relics, if you dared to look closer.

In 2026, Windmill came alive through the work of many hands, a collective of architects, builders, students, and community partners. In partnership with Portland affordable-housing nonprofit Sabin CDC, the neighborhood’s booths, bar, seating, and stage are built as a “kit of parts” made to go full circle: after the festival, the pieces move on to support Sabin’s placemaking, gardening, and community-building work across Portland. Waechter Architecture shaped the rest: forest rooms, a gateway, and a DJ stage from a single repeating module, each offering a rare chance to step out of the crowd, lie back, and look up at nothing but canopy and sky.
The barn itself doesn't change. The inside does: redesigned each year and mostly built by Mike Dunn, Pickathon's log designer.
Lucky is designed by Sherry Pendarvis, who owns the farm. It isn't rebuilt; it changes in small, meaningful ways every year.

In 2026, the Farmhouse took on a new dimension. The structures you pass through, designed by Bora Architecture & Interiors in partnership with Dream Big City, are part of a larger story. Story poles, archways, a busking stage, and the ticketing pavilion were built as modular pieces with a life beyond the festival. After Pickathon, they become part of Dream Plaza 2.0, a community skate and arts space coming to Portland’s Central Eastside. What passes through here carries something forward.

In 2026, Curation held five events, each for 100 guests. Rooted in the same spirit of discovery that has defined Pickathon for more than two decades, Curation brings guests closer to the artists honoring musical traditions, reshaping genres, and charting new directions for what comes next. Access took a Weekend Pickathon Pass or the corresponding Day Pass for the event date, plus a separate Curation ticket.
Friday Night Dinner, July 31, 6:30–8:00 PM

Cafe Olli and The Brothers Comatose come together to celebrate craftsmanship, community, and the traditions that bring people together. Nearly a decade after their first Pickathon appearance, The Brothers Comatose, a San Francisco-based bluegrass band came back to Pendarvis Farm. They return with a richer catalog, seasoned musicianship, and the infectious harmonies that have made them one of modern bluegrass’s most enduring acts. Known for seasonally driven cooking, house-made breads and pastries, and thoughtful sourcing from local farms and producers, Cafe Olli, the beloved Northeast Portland cafe and bakery, creates food meant to be shared. Paired with The Brothers Comatose’s harmony-rich blend of bluegrass, folk, and Americana, this gathering celebrates the simple pleasures of good food, good music, and good company. Setting the mood throughout is Country Co-Op, the Portland DJ collective whose vinyl-forward sets bring outlaw country, honky-tonk, and a back-porch spirit to the evening.
Saturday Brunch, August 1, 11:00 AM–12:30 PM
Chef Cathy Whims of Nostrana x Family Company

In 2026, The Refuge was inspired by the theme Coming Home, an invitation to journey through Oregon’s diverse bioregions while returning to what grounds us. Wander from a welcoming Willamette Valley farmstead into the towering Mt. Hood forest, exhale in the open High Desert, and follow the river to the Oregon Coast. Inspired by laundry lines and prayer flags, flowing textiles drift among the trees, a gentle reminder that our presence in nature can be light, temporary, and still deeply meaningful. Designed and built by Peter Mangano and Duke Stebbins, with decor by Glyness Dean.

Pickathon’s creativity doesn’t end when the music does. After Pickathon 2026, the wood used to build the Refuge Neighborhood was set to go to Alliance Charter Academy, a homeschool-hybrid charter school in Oregon City, where it would get a second life through hands-on learning.

The Coyote Neighborhood is a full kids’ festival tucked safely in the woods above Cherry Hill. In 2026 it became Captain Coyote’s Frog Bog, with stage sets, play structures and art installations designed by Cedarwood Waldorf School and Pickathon’s resident artists. The Coyote Stage runs all day Friday, Saturday and Sunday with performances by GRAMMY-winners, Portland favorites and family artists curated by Red Yarn. Beyond the stage: morning Family Yoga, music classes with Music Together of Portland and My Voice Music, wilderness adventures with Trackers Earth, drop-off childcare with Cedarwood Waldorf School, a nursing area hosted by Bridgetown Baby, crafts with Crafty Critters, collaborative art with Making Earth Cool, and a Sunday Puppet Parade. Programming spans newborns to teens, including a new teen volunteer program with Sellwood Community House.

In 2026, that plaza became a habitat. Two massive water lilies rise from the blacktop, built from layered lumber and stacked petal by petal into full bloom. By day they read as raw wood and geometry, monumental forms that invite you to sit and linger. By night, they ignite: light pours through the slats, a DJ drops in from inside one flower, and the other opens its arms to anyone who wants to dance. A habitat built for the night.
Designed by: Matt Thomas & Chris Cardoza Built by: Blackbird Public Arts Downstream partner: Guild of Oregon Woodworkers, Blackbird Public Arts

Mountains of Sound returns to Pickathon’s Market neighborhood for its second year as a circular timber pavilion built from 120 radiating frames, inspired by Wizard Island, the volcanic cinder cone at the center of Crater Lake. Designed by award-winning LA architecture studio West of West and structural engineers Holmes, the structure sweeps low at the center and rises at the outer edges to create shade, with benches along both the inner and outer edges inviting visitors to sit, look up through the interlocking frames, and find each other between sets. By day it functions as a shaded retreat and meeting point. After dark the dance floor activates, a DJ performs within the crowd, and sound fills the space from every direction.

The project was conceived from the outset as a future community asset, continuing Pickathon’s tradition of repurposing festival structures after the event, with past projects seeing stages transformed into sleeping pods for veterans and lumber donated to local high schools. As Jai Kumaran describes it: “Mountains of Sound is an installation designed to engage all your senses by creating rhythms of light and shadow throughout the day. And as you move through it, the experience moves with you, nothing is static. Every moment inside it is a different way of experiencing the music.”

In 2026, the path took on a new shape. Story poles and a series of archways designed by Bora Architecture & Interiors in partnership with Dream Big City line the way, each piece part of a longer journey from Pendarvis Farm to Dream Plaza 2.0, a community skate and arts space coming to Portland’s Central Eastside. The Orchard has always been a threshold. In 2026 it carried a little more with it.
